atv2-b1-p1.transcript: Today, Fantin's dance suites — specifically the set of manuscript parts kept at Welden. Start with their condition, because it surprised everyone. These are not working copies. The corners are crisp, there are no performers' markings, no wax, and what little rubbing exists is uniform from the first suite to the last. Nor can you blame later readers: there are no library stamps, no shelf wear, nothing added after the parts arrived. As far as we can tell, these parts were never played from at all — a set made to be looked at. Now, Casperi. Why does that court matter? One document: a letter written there in seventeen twenty-two, describing Fantin himself leading the suites from the violin — our only eyewitness account. Casperi's payment books never mention the suites, its band was about the same size as Welden's, and the printed dedication names the Duke of Welden, exactly as you would expect. The letter is the prize. Were these pieces for actual dancing? I say yes, and the scores tell you so themselves: the repeat schemes fit the surviving choreographies figure for figure, and that holds for every movement, first to last. The tempo markings are perfectly danceable, and the court ledger tells us nothing either way. Finally, the missing second-violin book. The editors will not invent the line themselves, and they refuse to print the suites with a hole in the texture. The rumored amateur copy has never been traced. So those suites wait — set aside for the final volume, once everything else is out.

explanations.q1: The professor says the parts show almost no signs of handling and were, as far as anyone can tell, never played from — a set made to be looked at, not working copies.
explanations.q2: Casperi matters for one document: a letter written there describing Fantin himself leading the suites from the violin, the only eyewitness account.
explanations.q3: The professor says yes because the scores themselves show it — the repeat schemes fit the surviving choreographies figure for figure.
explanations.q4: The professor says the suites touched by the missing book wait, set aside for the final volume once everything else is out.

q1.3: The professor clears the library explicitly: "there are no library stamps", no shelf wear, nothing added later.

q2.1: There is no contrast of forces to draw — its band was "about the same size" as Welden's.
q2.2: No dedication puzzle exists: the print "names the Duke of Welden", exactly as expected.

q3.2: No split repertory — the fit with the choreographies "holds for every movement", first to last.
q3.3: His evidence is in the scores, not the accounts: "the court ledger tells us nothing" either way.

q4.3: No copy is being acquired; the rumored amateur copy "has never been traced".

atv2-b1-p2.transcript: The Vasslen glacier. First, the eighteen-seventies advance. The lake cores finally settle its length, and the answer is odd: two distinct pushes. Between them the ice withdrew, and it stayed back long enough for a thin soil to start forming on the fresh moraine. So it did not hold the valley throughout, and the whole affair was far too drawn out to fit inside ten years. The maps that stretch it toward fifty years are simply misdated. Now the present advance, and here is my central point: this is a change at the bed, not in the budget. The surveys find no gain in mass anywhere on the glacier; the ice is simply sliding faster over its bed. No bulge is traveling down the ice from snowy winters past, the soundings off the front show clean deep water with nothing building there, and the tributary arms are as stagnant as ever. Faster sliding, same glacier. What next? The team means to winter over — keeping the station manned through the dark months for the first time. The stake line will stay where it is, the nineteen thirty-eight ridge stations were re-photographed two summers ago, and there will be no camera on the spur, which cannot be serviced in winter. Last, the Ravnas farm. From its yard, someone drew the glacier in seventeen ninety-four — the earliest picture of the ice that we possess. The farm's account books are lost, no grazing quarrel there ever came to law, and the family never sold so much as a block of ice. But that sketch is where the whole record begins.

explanations.q1: The lake cores show two distinct pushes with the ice withdrawn between them long enough for a thin soil to start forming.
explanations.q2: The professor's central point is a change at the bed: no gain in mass anywhere, the ice simply sliding faster over its bed.
explanations.q3: The team means to winter over, keeping the station manned through the dark months for the first time.
explanations.q4: The Ravnas farm matters because a sketch drawn from its yard in 1794 is the earliest picture of the ice that survives.

q1.1: One continuous generation-long occupation cannot stand: the ice "did not hold the valley throughout"; there was a pause with soil forming.
q1.3: The half-century version is dismissed as a dating error — the maps that "stretch it toward fifty years" are misdated.

q2.1: The lagged-snowfall account is denied in so many words: "No bulge is traveling down the ice".
q2.2: Soundings kill the sediment-bank idea — off the front there is "clean deep water" with nothing building.
q2.3: No reconnected arm is feeding the trunk; the tributary arms are "as stagnant as ever".

q3.0: Extending the stake network is off: "The stake line will stay where it is".
q3.1: The repeat photography is already done, "re-photographed two summers ago", so it cannot be next season's plan.
q3.3: The camera plan is explicitly dead — "no camera on the spur", which cannot be serviced in winter.

q4.3: The ice trade never existed — the family "never sold so much as a block of ice".

atv2-b1-p3.transcript: Every year I put one page of the Ostrand ledgers on screen, for the same reason: there, in a single column, barter sits beside coin. A farmer settles in rye; the next line is silver; nobody blinks. That mixing is what I want you to see. The hand, by the way, is the founder's throughout — his son never kept these books — the notation is plain and needs no decoding, and you cannot chase these entries into letters, because the correspondence for those years was burned. Just the mixing. Now, the spike of seventeen sixty-eight. The price series built from these ledgers is stark: the rise appears everywhere at once. Coast, uplands, market towns — within days of one another, which for that century is simultaneity. The inland towns did not lead, the ports did not lead, and nothing hopped from town to town; there was no sequence to find. And the partners? At the height, the letters show them carrying. Their ships spent the crisis hauling other houses' grain for freight fees — steady money, no exposure. They never sold out early to watch from shore, timber never tempted them, and the city never engaged them to buy on its account. Carriers, by choice. Which leaves the old story of a merchant ring withholding grain. I dismiss it, on arithmetic alone: no ring could have warehoused enough to move prices beyond a week. The letters give no sign any house held grain back at any stage, the storage registers for those years are lost, and no papers are waiting in a notary's files.

explanations.q1: The page goes up for one reason: in a single column, barter sits beside coin — rye on one line, silver on the next.
explanations.q2: The series shows the rise appearing everywhere at once — coast, uplands, market towns within days of one another.
explanations.q3: The letters show the partners carrying: their ships spent the crisis hauling other houses' grain for freight fees.
explanations.q4: The professor dismisses the ring story on arithmetic alone — no ring could have warehoused enough to move prices beyond a week.

q1.0: There is nothing to decipher — the notation is plain and "needs no decoding", so that cannot be the lesson.
q1.2: Tracing an entry outward is impossible: "the correspondence for those years was burned".
q1.3: No change of hand exists to show; the founder wrote throughout and "his son never kept these books".

q2.0: The inland-first pattern is denied point-blank: "The inland towns did not lead".
q2.2: A port-led spread fares no better — "the ports did not lead", and the uplands rose with everyone else.
q2.3: There was no town-by-town sequence, random or otherwise: nothing "hopped from town to town".

q3.0: They did not sit the rise out; the partners "never sold out early" to watch from shore.
q3.1: The timber move never happened — "timber never tempted them".
q3.2: No public commission existed: the city never engaged them "to buy on its account".

q4.0: He credits nothing of the sort, and "no papers are waiting" in a notary's files to change the picture.
q4.2: The reactive-withholding reading dies with the rest: the letters give no sign any house "held grain back at any stage".
q4.3: His dismissal cannot rest on the registers, because "the storage registers for those years are lost".

atv2-b1-p4.transcript: Five years ago the spawning grounds shifted from the Herta Bank to the shallows off Vindo, and the tag returns finally give us the shape of it. The split runs by age. The older fish led the move — they were over the new ground almost at once — while the younger fish stayed put on the old bank for several seasons before following. And the returns come from just those two grounds, nowhere else. Why the move? Here is my main point, and I will defend it: seals. A colony has settled the skerries beside the old bank, and it hunts the shoals precisely when they gather. The gravel there is as clean as it ever was, the temperatures over the old ground have not changed in any season that matters, and the bloom arrives when it always has — the larvae would still be fed there. What changed is that gathering became dangerous. Next year's survey reflects all this. Over the roughest ground the towed cameras have been useless, so divers will work those stretches instead. The old bank stays in the rotation — we drop nothing — the institute's own vessel sails as always, and no other institute is involved. One more thing: the jars in the basement. Those preserved samples include ripe fish taken over Vindo seventy years before monitoring began, so the new ground is not new at all. It is a small holding, mind you — too few specimens to trace any change in the fish themselves — but the labels are impeccable, and the jars were never in any danger during the renovations.

explanations.q1: The tag returns split by age: the older fish were over the new ground almost at once while the younger stayed on the old bank for several seasons.
explanations.q2: Because the towed cameras have been useless over the roughest ground, divers will work those stretches in next year's survey.
explanations.q3: The jars matter because they include ripe fish taken over Vindo seventy years before monitoring began — the new ground is not new.
explanations.q4: The professor's main point is the seal colony on the skerries beside the old bank, hunting the shoals precisely when they gather.

q1.1: A one-season wholesale transfer is contradicted: the younger fish stayed put "for several seasons" before following.
q1.3: No scattering happened; the returns come "from just those two grounds", nowhere else.

q2.0: Nothing is being dropped from the survey — "The old bank stays in the rotation".

q2.3: A joint operation is excluded outright: "no other institute is involved".

q3.2: There is no rescue story to tell; the jars were "never in any danger" during the renovations.
q3.3: Mislabeling is denied in passing: "the labels are impeccable".

q4.3: The food timing is unchanged; the bloom "arrives when it always has", so the larvae would still be fed there.

atv2-b1-p5.transcript: When Gravenstad pulled down its walls, the council took forty years over it — and that, I will argue, was wisdom. Each section came down only when the city could pay for it out of ordinary revenue, so the demolition left no debt behind. The plan of eighteen twelve was followed section by section, and the council never once reversed itself. Nor was it pushed from below: the record shows not one breach forced by townspeople ahead of the crews. And the contracts went to outside firms, at close to the original estimates. Deliberate, solvent, slow. Who moved onto the cleared ring first? The tax rolls answer: innkeepers. Travelers no longer had to lodge beyond the gates, and the inns caught them at the new openings. The weavers stayed inside the town for another generation, gardeners never appear on the ring parcels at all, and the hospital kept to its medieval site until the century's end. Inns first. Now, the visiting engineer's report of eighteen thirty-one. I quote it for its dedication — three pages of flattery to the burgomasters. That is the genre: such reports were auditions, bids for a city's business dressed up as expertise. The man surveyed the walls only in passing, the report contains no drawings at all, and he never worked for Gravenstad again; the promenade was laid out by another hand entirely. And the rents? Once the ring opened, rents fell right across the old center, fronts and courts alike, as wealthy households moved to the edge. They did not climb anywhere inside the old line. The fall is unbroken in the series.

explanations.q1: The professor argues the forty-year pace was wisdom: each section came down only when the city could pay from ordinary revenue, leaving no debt.
explanations.q2: The tax rolls answer innkeepers — travelers no longer had to lodge beyond the gates, and the inns caught them at the new openings.
explanations.q3: The report is quoted for its three pages of flattery: such reports were auditions, bids for a city's business dressed up as expertise.
explanations.q4: The rent series shows rents falling right across the old center, fronts and courts alike, as wealthy households moved to the edge.

q1.1: The council was not trailing events; the record shows "not one breach" forced by townspeople ahead of the crews.
q1.2: No insider dealing: the contracts went "to outside firms", at close to the original estimates.
q1.3: Far from drifting, the plan was followed section by section and the council "never once reversed itself".

q2.1: The weavers came late, not first — they "stayed inside the town" for another generation.
q2.2: Gardeners are absent from the record: they "never appear on the ring parcels" at all.
q2.3: The hospital did not take ring land; it "kept to its medieval site" until the century's end.

q3.0: It is no survey of record — the man "surveyed the walls only in passing".
q3.1: There are no demolition sketches to consult; the report "contains no drawings" at all.
q3.2: The author's later career is cut off explicitly: he "never worked for Gravenstad again", and the promenade was laid out by another hand.

q4.1: The series is not flat — "The fall is unbroken" in the series once the ring opened.
q4.2: A rise is excluded everywhere: rents "did not climb anywhere" inside the old line.
q4.3: No front-versus-court split appears; rents fell "fronts and courts alike".

atv2-b1-p6.transcript: TW Corvi's disk, and the dark ring everyone argues about. Some history first. The Kestler program observed this star for years, and its survey paper describes the disk as smooth — featureless, no structure at all. I mention it to calibrate you: twenty years on, the Aldan Array resolves the same disk in exquisite detail. That is how far the instruments have come. Note the disk itself was found decades before Kestler ever ran, and the new measurements stand on their own calibration — they owe nothing to Kestler's standards. So what does the Array show? The gap sits just where the models put it, and its width matches the predictions closely. It is one opening — no bright strand divides it. What is new is the profile: the inner edge is cut like a cliff, while the outer edge fades away by slow degrees. A cliff and a fade is what a cast shadow does. There is a warp in the inner disk, and the dark zone, I claim, is simply poorly lit — not empty. The spectral slope points to ordinary-sized grains all through the zone: cold, shaded, but there. No ice condenses at that radius, and a companion big enough to sweep the zone would disturb the neighboring belts, which sit serenely undisturbed. What next? Waiting, honestly. The receivers are being upgraded, and the team will not observe again until that work is finished. No new time proposal is going in, the data stay in-house until the paper is out, and there are no plans to survey other stars. Patience, for once.

explanations.q1: Kestler's survey paper called the disk featureless, and the professor uses that miss to mark how far the instruments have come in twenty years.
explanations.q2: The new observations show the profile: the inner edge cut like a cliff while the outer edge fades away by slow degrees.
explanations.q3: The professor claims a warp in the inner disk casts a shadow, so the dark zone is simply poorly lit, not empty.
explanations.q4: The team will not observe again until the receiver upgrade is finished — no proposal, no release, no survey, just waiting.

q1.1: Discovery credit is placed elsewhere — the disk was found "decades before Kestler ever ran".
q1.2: No calibration dependence exists; the new measurements "owe nothing to Kestler's standards".

q2.0: The gap is not oversized: its "width matches the predictions" closely.
q2.1: The double-gap reading is denied — it is one opening, and "no bright strand divides it".
q2.3: Its location is as modeled, sitting "just where the models put it".

q3.0: Dynamics forbid the companion: a body big enough to sweep the zone "would disturb the neighboring belts", which sit serenely undisturbed.
q3.1: The ice-line story fails on location — "No ice condenses at that radius".
q3.2: The grains are not hiding by size; the spectral slope "points to ordinary-sized grains" all through the zone.

q4.1: An early release is ruled out — the data "stay in-house until the paper is out".
q4.2: A comparison campaign is denied flatly: there are "no plans to survey other stars".

atv2-b1-p7.transcript: The Tarei valley bands. The looms are busy — everyday cloth is made in every hamlet, and it is woven in the valley itself, not bought in from downriver. But the marriage patterns are another matter: those designs have been retired. Nobody has set one on a loom in two generations. The old bands still move through marriage payments; no new ones join them. Weaving lives; that one repertoire is closed. Now, the district officer's inventory of nineteen-oh-two. Its value is a fact people overlook: it lists bands held by families three districts away. The things had traveled far beyond the valley before any ethnographer arrived. That is all I want from it — it records no prices and no livestock equivalents, it had nothing to do with taxation, since the officer compiled it for a museum, and every pattern it names can be matched to a surviving band. How is a band's worth judged? Our fieldwork was unambiguous: by the hand. Elders roll the cloth between finger and thumb, and tightness is everything. A band's pedigree counts for little — nobody we asked cared much who wove a piece — no motif outranks another, and a new band, well woven, stands above a darkened old one. Finally, Marovic. Handle his monograph with tongs. On the loom, on technique, he is exact; we can verify him knot for knot. On exchange he matches nothing we recorded. His informants, the elders insist, dealt with him honestly, and what he described was no passing fashion of his decade. The failure was his own, and it sits squarely in the exchange chapters.

explanations.q1: Everyday cloth is still woven in every hamlet, but the marriage designs have been retired — nobody has set one on a loom in two generations.
explanations.q2: The inventory's value is that it lists bands held three districts away, showing the things had traveled far beyond the valley by 1902.
explanations.q3: Fieldwork was unambiguous: worth is judged by the hand — elders roll the cloth between finger and thumb, and tightness is everything.
explanations.q4: Marovic is exact on the loom and technique but matches nothing the team recorded on exchange — split down the middle.

q1.1: Weaving as such never ended: "The looms are busy" with everyday cloth in every hamlet.
q1.2: Production has not migrated; the cloth is "woven in the valley itself", not bought in from downriver.

atv2-b1-p8.transcript: The Brenner quarry bonebed. You have read the isotope paper claiming the herd walked in from far away. I am setting that conclusion aside, and here is why: every reference value in the study comes from the Aldfeld basin, whose geology is nothing like ours. Against the wrong baseline the numbers support no reading at all — and I mean none; I am not offering some story about changing local water instead. The method is sound, and burial has not touched this material. There is also no point running the other species against the same flawed baseline. Fix the baseline first. The mapping shows a pattern I trust more. Complete skeletons crowd the middle of the bed, and the bone grows more scattered toward the rim — a smooth gradient, with no clustering into groups anywhere. The carcasses point every which way, and the small bones are all present, down to the last toe. Whatever happened here happened in place. What next? We are closing the excavation. The exposure will be covered and held until techniques catch up, a decision I support. The flooded gallery stays flooded, nobody is going prospecting on the plain, and no shelter will be built. Digging is stopping, not growing. Finally, the railway workers who found all this in eighteen ninety-one. I tell their story as a warning: they kept no notes. The cut itself clipped only the lowest meter of the bed, the men left no letters, and everything they collected stayed in this country, in three museums. But because nothing was written down, the upper part of the bed cannot be placed today.

explanations.q1: The professor sets the conclusion aside because every reference value comes from the Aldfeld basin, whose geology is nothing like the quarry's.
explanations.q2: The mapping shows complete skeletons crowding the middle of the bed with bone growing more scattered toward the rim — a smooth gradient.
explanations.q3: The excavation is closing: the exposure will be covered and held until techniques catch up.
explanations.q4: The discovery story is a warning — the workers kept no notes, which is why the upper part of the bed cannot be placed today.

q1.2: Far from endorsing an extension, he sees no point "running the other species" against the same flawed baseline.
q1.3: His objection is not to the technique — the method is sound, and "burial has not touched" this material.

q2.2: Nothing small is missing — "the small bones are all present", down to the last toe.
q2.3: The bed does not resolve into groups: a smooth gradient, with "no clustering into groups" anywhere.

q3.3: Year-round work is the opposite of the plan: "no shelter will be built", and digging is stopping, not growing.
